abstract.text: Abstract. A new notion of equilibrium, which we call strong equilibrium, is introduced for time-inconsistent stopping problems in continuous time. Compared to the existing notions introduced in (Huang & Nguyen-Huu, 2018) and (Christensen & Lindensjö, 2018), which in this paper are called mild equilibrium and weak equilibrium respectively, a strong equilibrium captures the idea of subgame perfect Nash equilibrium more accurately. When the state process is a continuoustime Markov chain and the discount function is log sub-additive, we show that an optimal mild equilibrium is always a strong equilibrium. Moreover, we provide a new iteration method that can directly construct an optimal mild equilibrium and thus also prove its existence.

sections.summary: Introduces the problem of time-inconsistent stopping in continuous time, reviews pre-commitment, naive, and consistent-planning approaches, and defines mild, optimal mild, weak, and strong equilibria. The section argues that existing mild and weak notions understate the economic meaning of equilibrium and motivates strong equilibrium as capturing subgame-perfect Nash behavior more accurately.

abstract.text: Abstract. A new notion of equilibrium, which we call strong equilibrium, is introduced for time-inconsistent stopping problems in continuous time. Compared to the existing notions introduced in (Huang & Nguyen-Huu, 2018) and (Christensen & Lindensjö, 2018), which in this paper are called mild equilibrium and weak equilibrium respectively, a strong equilibrium captures the idea of subgame perfect Nash equilibrium more accurately. When the state process is a continuoustime Markov chain and the discount function is log sub-additive, we show that an optimal mild equilibrium is always a strong equilibrium. Moreover, we provide a new iteration method that can directly construct an optimal mild equilibrium and thus also prove its existence.

sections.summary: Introduces the problem of time-inconsistent stopping in continuous time, reviews pre-commitment, naive, and consistent-planning approaches, and defines mild, optimal mild, weak, and strong equilibria. The section argues that existing mild and weak notions understate the economic meaning of equilibrium and motivates strong equilibrium as capturing subgame-perfect Nash behavior more accurately.
